script.opening: “Hi, thanks for calling back. I had a miscarriage two weeks ago — I did the tablets at home. I did a pregnancy test this morning and it’s still positive. Faint, but positive. Is something wrong? Is there still something in there?”

facts.text: Confirms date of birth if asked. At home, on her own — “Tunde’s at work.” Fine to talk.

“I had a scan at nine weeks because of spotting and they said there was no heartbeat. The baby had stopped growing at about seven weeks. I chose the tablets at home. I bled a lot that day and passed… everything, I think. It was awful.”
If asked: light brown spotting, “like the end of a period”, a pad lasts all day. No clots now. Mild cramps sometimes, paracetamol helps. No fever, no shivers, no smelly discharge. Not dizzy or faint.
If asked what the EPAU told her: “To do a test after three weeks. I couldn’t wait. I just wanted to know it was over.”
If asked: “I’m Rhesus negative. Last time they gave me an injection, but this time they said I didn’t need it. Is that right?”

“I lost one last March at seven weeks too. Two now. Does that mean there’s something wrong with me?” No live births. Periods regular before. Not on any medicines. No medical problems. Non-smoker. BMI “about 25”.
If asked about plans: “We want to try again. I’m 33 — I feel like time is running out. How long do we have to wait?” Was taking folic acid before.
If asked how she is feeling: “Numb. Then crying in the car. I’m not sleeping.” If asked directly: no thoughts of harming herself — “No. I just feel empty.” Has not told her mother or friends.
Off work for a week after, went back last week. “The children are lovely but I keep having to leave the room.”

Only if asked whether she has any thoughts about why it happened: “We were moving classrooms — I carried heavy boxes the week before. And I had a glass of wine at a birthday before I knew I was pregnant. Was it me?” Only if asked about her partner or support: “Tunde went straight back to work like nothing happened. He doesn’t talk about it. I feel like I’m on my own.”

Anxious and tearful but articulate. Lead with the test. If the doctor only deals with the test and ends the call, say “OK…” flatly and end. If the doctor asks how she is or why she thinks it happened, let the guilt and loneliness out. Respond with relief to a clear explanation that it was not her fault. If the doctor offers practical help (fit note, support, a follow-up call, something for Tunde), say “That would really help.”

ice.ideas: “Maybe there’s still something left inside. Maybe I did something to cause it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she blames herself (heavy boxes at work, a glass of wine before she knew) and fears two losses mean she cannot have a baby; she feels alone because her partner has gone back to work and won’t talk about it. She shares this only if asked about causes, her feelings or support.
ice.expectations: To know whether the positive test is a problem; to know when they can try again and whether she needs tests.

cues: “I just wanted to know it was over” — grief and need for closure behind the early test.
“Two now. Does that mean there’s something wrong with me?” — fear about future pregnancy.
“Numb. Then crying in the car.” — emotional impact; ask about support and mood.

checkpoints.text: Confirms identity and privacy, then checks for red flags of retained tissue or infection: heavy bleeding, clots, worsening pain, fever, offensive discharge, dizziness — none present
Clarifies the history: missed miscarriage at 9 weeks, medical management at home 16 days ago, tissue passed, second loss, RhD negative, and the EPAU instruction to test at 3 weeks

Explains that a faint positive test at 2 weeks can be normal as pregnancy hormone falls gradually; advises repeating the test at 3 weeks and contacting EPAU if still positive (possible incomplete miscarriage, rarely molar pregnancy), and explains why anti-D was not needed under current NICE guidance
Explores her ideas about cause and specifically the self-blame (lifting, wine), and asks about mood, sleep, thoughts of self-harm, support and her partner
Explains clearly that most early miscarriages are caused by chromosomal problems in the pregnancy and are not caused by work, lifting, exercise, sex or a small amount of alcohol before knowing

Advises on the next pregnancy: no medical need to wait beyond feeling ready (often after the next period for dating), folic acid, early pregnancy unit self-referral for an early scan, progesterone if bleeding in a future pregnancy with a previous miscarriage; discusses recurrent pregnancy loss assessment after two losses

Offers practical and emotional support: fit note if needed, Miscarriage Association and Tommy’s, NHS Talking Therapies, the optional pregnancy loss certificate, support for her partner, and a follow-up call; safety-nets clearly
Acknowledges the loss as a bereavement, uses warm, non-medical language (“your baby”, if she does), allows emotion, and avoids minimising (“at least it was early”)

worked.txt: “I’m so sorry about your loss. Before we talk about the test — how much are you bleeding now, any strong pain, fever, or smelly discharge?”

“After a miscarriage the pregnancy hormone falls gradually, so at two weeks a faint positive can be normal. That’s why the unit asked you to test at three weeks. If it’s still positive then, call them — they’ll check that everything has come away.”

“Most early miscarriages happen because the baby’s chromosomes didn’t develop as they should — it’s decided very early and nothing you did caused it. Carrying boxes and a glass of wine before you knew don’t cause a miscarriage.”

“Two losses is heartbreaking, and it’s more common than people realise. Most people with two losses go on to have a baby. Guidance now suggests looking into it after two losses, so I’d like to talk about a referral to the recurrent miscarriage service.”

“There’s no medical reason to wait once you feel ready. Keep taking folic acid. Next time you can refer yourself to the early pregnancy unit for an early scan, and if you bleed, there’s a hormone treatment called progesterone that can help.”
“How are you really doing? … And how is Tunde? Men often grieve differently and throw themselves into work — it doesn’t mean he doesn’t care. Would it help if I sent you both some information?”

f.learning: A telephone follow-up after early miscarriage has a safety part and a human part. Safety: screen for heavy bleeding, pain, fever and offensive discharge; after medical or expectant management NICE NG126 advises a urine pregnancy test at 3 weeks, with review if positive — a faint positive at 2 weeks is often normal. Anti-D is no longer recommended for miscarriage up to 11+6 weeks (NG126, 2026 update). The human part: treat it as a bereavement, address self-blame directly (most losses are chromosomal and not caused by anything she did), advise on the next pregnancy, discuss assessment after two losses, check mood and partner support, and offer practical help and follow-up.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management (2019, updated June 2026) · RCOG Green-top Guideline 17 Recurrent miscarriage (2023) · NHS England pregnancy loss certificate service (launched 2024) · Miscarriage Association and Tommy’s patient information · NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health (2014, updated 2020)
knowledge.summary: Faint positive test 16 days after medical management, with no red flags: retest at 3 weeks. Then the real work — guilt, two losses, next pregnancy, mood and support.

points.t: Heavy bleeding (soaking a pad an hour), large clots, worsening pain, fever, offensive discharge or feeling faint suggest retained tissue or infection — same-day EPAU or A&E.

After expectant or medical management, NICE NG126 advises a urine pregnancy test 3 weeks later; if positive, return for individualised care (incomplete miscarriage, or rarely gestational trophoblastic disease).

NICE NG126 (June 2026) no longer recommends anti-D prophylaxis for miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy up to and including 11+6 weeks — this replaces earlier advice to give anti-D after surgical management.

About 1 in 4–5 recognised pregnancies end in miscarriage; most early losses are due to chromosomal abnormality. Work, lifting, exercise, sex, stress or a small amount of alcohol before knowing do not cause miscarriage. Risk rises with maternal age and smoking.

RCOG (2023) defines recurrent pregnancy loss as two or more losses and supports a graded approach to assessment; local services vary in what they offer after two losses. Tests may include antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid function and pelvic ultrasound.

No medical need to wait beyond emotional readiness; folic acid 400 micrograms (5 mg if indicated); early scan through EPAU; NICE NG126: offer vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily to women with bleeding in early pregnancy and a previous miscarriage once an intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed.

Grief, anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms are common after miscarriage, in both partners. Ask about mood and self-harm; offer NHS Talking Therapies and charity support; consider a follow-up call.
Fit note if needed (self-certify up to 7 days); the optional pregnancy loss certificate for losses before 24 weeks in England; return-to-work conversation; contraception if not trying.

model.text: Hello, is that Nkechi? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth, and is it a good time to talk privately?
model.why: Identity and privacy on the telephone

model.text: Yes. I had a miscarriage two weeks ago, the tablets at home. I did a test this morning and it’s still positive. Is something wrong?
I’m so sorry about your loss. Let me check you’re safe first. How much are you bleeding now — any clots, strong pain, fever, smelly discharge, or feeling faint?
Just light brown spotting. Mild cramps. No fever, nothing smelly.

That’s reassuring. The pregnancy hormone falls gradually, so at two weeks a faint positive can be normal. That’s why the unit asked for a test at three weeks. If it’s still positive then, ring them so they can check everything has come away.
model.why: Explains the test result and the plan

model.text: I just wanted to know it was over. And they said I didn’t need the anti-D this time — is that right? Last time I had it.
Yes, that’s right. National guidance changed this year: for miscarriages before 12 weeks the evidence showed the injection isn’t needed. You’ve had the right care.
You said you wanted to know it was over. How are you doing with all of this?
Numb. Then crying in the car. Not sleeping. Two now — is something wrong with me?
That sounds so hard. Do you have any thoughts about why it might have happened?
I carried heavy boxes at work. And I had a glass of wine before I knew. Was it me?

No — it wasn’t you. Most early miscarriages happen because the baby’s chromosomes didn’t form properly, right at the start. Lifting boxes and a glass of wine before you knew don’t cause a miscarriage.
(Crying.) Thank you. I needed to hear that.
Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself? And who’s supporting you — how is Tunde?
No, nothing like that. Tunde went straight back to work like nothing happened. I feel on my own.

Partners often grieve differently and bury themselves in work — it doesn’t mean he doesn’t care. I’ll send you information from the Miscarriage Association that includes partners. About the future: there’s no medical need to wait once you feel ready; keep up the folic acid; next time refer yourself to the early pregnancy unit for an early scan, and if you bleed there’s progesterone treatment that can help. After two losses I’d like to refer you to the recurrent miscarriage service to talk about tests. Would that be OK?
model.why: Next pregnancy, recurrent loss and partner support

model.text: Yes, please. I want to know.

If the bleeding gets heavy, you get bad pain, a fever or a smelly discharge, call the early pregnancy unit or 111, or 999 if you feel faint. Test again on day 21. You can also have a fit note, there’s talking therapy you can refer yourself to, and an optional pregnancy loss certificate if you’d like one. I’ll call you in two weeks. What will you do next?
model.why: Safety-net, practical support, follow-up and teach-back

model.text: Test again next week, call the unit if positive, and you’ll call me. And I’ll look at the Miscarriage Association with Tunde.

social.t: Early loss is often unseen by others; many women have not told family or colleagues and return to work quickly.
Partners can feel excluded and cope by working; offering resources for both reduces isolation.
Teaching young children can be painful after a loss; a fit note or phased return may help.

legal.t: In England, parents who lose a pregnancy before 24 weeks can request an optional, non-statutory certificate to recognise their loss.
Sickness related to pregnancy loss should be recorded separately by employers; check current employment rights for bereavement leave.

professional.t: Follow the patient’s language (“my baby” or “the pregnancy”); avoid “at least it was early” and medical terms like “products of conception” on the phone.
Record the loss accurately so future contacts (cervical screening, invitations, antenatal letters) are sensitive.

community.t: Miscarriage Association (helpline and partner resources), Tommy’s, Sands, NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), local EPAU counselling.

redFlags: Heavy bleeding or clots, feeling faint
ice: Idea: something left inside; she caused it
Concern: two losses mean infertility; feeling alone
Expectation: is the test a problem; when to try again; tests

playbook.diagnosis: Recovery after medical management of a missed miscarriage at 9 weeks, with an expected faint positive pregnancy test at 16 days and no red flags; second consecutive early loss.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A faint positive at two weeks can be normal — the hormone takes a few weeks to go. We’ll check it at three weeks.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to know it was over — and you wanted to know it wasn’t your fault. It wasn’t.”
management.psychosocial: Bereavement support, partner resources, mood check, fit note, Talking Therapies.
sharedPlan: Repeat urine pregnancy test on day 21; EPAU if positive
Folic acid; early EPAU scan next time; progesterone if bleeding
safetyNet: Heavy bleeding, severe pain, fever, smelly discharge — EPAU/111; faint or collapse — 999
Low mood worsening or thoughts of self-harm — contact GP same day or 111 option 2

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating it purely as a pregnancy-test query and ending the call — or by giving outdated advice.

items.fail: Discussing the test without screening for bleeding, pain or infection.
items.why: Retained tissue and infection must be excluded.

items.fail: Sending her for an urgent scan for a faint positive at 2 weeks.
items.why: Not in line with NG126 and causes distress.
items.fix: Retest at 3 weeks; EPAU if positive.

items.fail: Telling her she should have had anti-D.
items.why: Outdated — NG126 (2026) no longer recommends it up to 11+6 weeks.
items.fix: Reassure that she had the right care.

items.fail: Not asking what she thinks caused it.
items.why: Misses the self-blame that drives her distress.
items.fix: “Do you have any thoughts about why it happened?”

items.fail: No plan for the future or for two losses.
items.why: Her main fear is future pregnancy.
items.fix: Next-pregnancy advice and recurrent loss referral.

wordPics.clearFail: Deals only with the test, or gives wrong advice (urgent scan, anti-D needed); no red-flag screen; minimises the loss.
wordPics.fail: Safe advice about the test but misses the self-blame, the partner issue or the future-pregnancy questions; vague support.
wordPics.pass: Screens red flags, explains the test and retest at 3 weeks, addresses cause and guilt, advises on next pregnancy and offers support and safety-net.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: accurate anti-D update, explicit discussion of two losses with referral, mood and self-harm check, partner support, practical help (fit note, certificate), follow-up call and teach-back — delivered with warmth.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: accurate anti-D update, explicit discussion of two losses with referral, mood and self-harm check, partner support, practical help (fit note, certificate), follow-up call and teach-back — delivered with warmth.
